instruction: TASK: Based on the parent's statement, describe the child's eye contact patterns in a clinical tone
Input 1: Yes, she did look at me. I remember she would always turn her head to see me when I came in, and if we were playing together, she’d check my face a lot, especially if she wasn’t sure about something. She also did it with her dad and her grandparents, and even at preschool, her teacher mentioned she was very engaged with people.
Predicted Summary 1: At the age of 4 to 5, Name used eye contact to communicate needs, but it was not sustained. Her caregiver noted that she would always turn her head to see her when she came, and she would check her face when playing together, especially if she wasn’t sure about something. Her teacher noted that she was highly engaged with people, including with her parents and grandparents.
Reference Summary 1: Name makes eye contact when seeking reassurance but generally avoids it during routine activities and peer interactions in school settings.
Input 2: Hmm… I don’t know. I never really thought about it before. I mean, I guess he must have looked at me sometimes, right? But now that I think about it, I can’t really remember specific times. I know he was very into his own thing, though—like, if he was playing with his blocks, he’d be totally absorbed. I don’t think he really checked in with me the way some other kids do.
Predicted Summary 2: At the age of 4 to 5, Name’s eye contact was inconsistent. His caregiver reported that he would occasionally look at her during moments of excitement, but he did not consistently check with her during play.
Reference Summary 2: At the age of 4 to 5, Name's eye contact was not a prominent feature of his interactions. His caregiver acknowledged that while he must have looked at her at times, it wasn’t something she specifically remembered. He was often deeply absorbed in his own activities, such as playing with blocks, and did not frequently check in with her the way some other children might. This suggested that Name's focus was more on his individual activities rather than on engaging through eye contact.
Input 3: Well, that’s tricky, because I guess I never really thought about it at the time. I mean, I knew he wasn’t really looking at people much, but I thought he was just a little shy. Like, he’d look up if I said his name, but he wouldn’t really hold eye contact. And if we were doing something together, sometimes he’d look, sometimes he wouldn’t. And with other people, well, I don’t think he was super interested in looking at them either. But he was very focused on what he liked—he could sit for hours sorting his cars, and nothing else mattered.
Predicted Summary 3: At the age of 4 to 5, Name made limited eye contact and often appeared disengaged. His caregiver noted that he was a little shy and rarely looked at others’ faces. His caregiver noted that he was very focused on what he liked, and he did not seem to be particularly interested in looking at others’ faces.
Reference Summary 3: Name uses eye contact instrumentally when requesting desired items. Eye contact is otherwise absent in both individual and group settings.
